questions.q: Quick Sort always picks the FIRST element as the pivot and is given the already sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. What is its running time on inputs like this?
choices: Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
questions.explain: The pivot is always the smallest element, so every partition is as unbalanced as possible. The work is n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2, which is Θ(n^2).

questions.q: First-element-pivot Quick Sort runs on the sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Using the work sum n + (n-1) + ... + 1, what is the total work?
Randomized Quick Sort is partitioning a subarray of 12 elements. What is the probability that one particular element is chosen as the pivot? Give a decimal.
questions.explain: Each of the n positions is equally likely, so each one has probability 1/n = 1/12 ≈ 0.0833.

questions.q: True or false: choosing the pivot at random brings Quick Sort's worst-case running time down to Θ(n log n).
questions.explain: The worst case is still Θ(n^2), because the random choices could keep landing on bad pivots. Randomization improves the EXPECTED running time to Θ(n log n).

questions.q: Which pair correctly gives the worst-case and expected running times of Randomized Quick Sort?
choices: Worst case Θ(n^2); expected Θ(n log n)
Worst case Θ(n log n); expected Θ(n log n)
Worst case Θ(n^2); expected Θ(n^2)
Worst case Θ(n log n); expected Θ(n^2)
questions.explain: A long run of bad pivots is still possible, so the worst case stays Θ(n^2). Because that run is unlikely, the expected time is Θ(n log n).

questions.q: Picture the values split as 25% | 50% | 25%. Which pivots count as "good" for Quick Sort?
choices: Only the exact median
Any pivot from the middle 50% of the values
Any pivot from the bottom 25% of the values
Only the smallest or largest value
questions.explain: You don't need the exact median. A pivot from the middle 50% gives a reasonably balanced split (neither side gets more than about 75%). The goal is to get enough good pivots, not perfect ones.

questions.q: True or false: if Randomized Quick Sort runs twice on the same input array, it always picks the same pivots both times.
questions.explain: The pivots are chosen at random, so the same input can lead to different pivot choices and different amounts of work. The output is correctly sorted either way.

questions.q: Why does picking the pivot at random help Quick Sort?
choices: It guarantees that every pivot is the median
It makes a long sequence of bad pivot choices unlikely, so no single input reliably triggers the slow case
It removes the need to partition the array
It makes Quick Sort run in linear time
questions.explain: A fixed rule such as 'always take the first element' can be beaten by one specific input, like a sorted array. With random pivots, a long run of bad choices is unlikely, so the expected time is Θ(n log n).

questions.q: What is a randomized algorithm?
choices: An algorithm whose input must be randomly ordered before it runs
An algorithm that deliberately uses randomness as part of its decision-making
An algorithm that returns a random output, ignoring its input
Any algorithm whose running time is Θ(n log n)
questions.explain: A randomized algorithm deliberately makes random choices while it runs. Choosing a random pivot in Quick Sort is one example.

questions.q: Randomized Quick Sort is an example of which kind of randomized algorithm?
choices: Monte Carlo
Las Vegas
Neither; it is deterministic
Both equally
questions.explain: Las Vegas: the array always ends up correctly sorted, but different random pivots mean different amounts of work, so the running time varies.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes a Monte Carlo algorithm?
choices: Answer: always correct. Runtime: may vary.
Answer: may vary between runs. Runtime: usually controlled or bounded.
Answer: always correct. Runtime: always the same.
Answer: may vary. Runtime: unbounded.
questions.explain: In Monte Carlo algorithms, randomness affects the answer and the runtime is usually controlled. In Las Vegas algorithms, the answer is always correct and the time may vary.

questions.q: True or false: a Las Vegas algorithm always produces the correct answer, but the time it takes can vary from run to run.
questions.explain: That is the definition of a Las Vegas algorithm: randomness affects the time, not whether the answer is correct.

questions.q: In the Monte Carlo sampling pseudocode (S := 0; for i := 1 to n: run the simulation, S := S + X_i; then m := S / n), five runs give X_1 = 6, X_2 = 9, X_3 = 3, X_4 = 7, X_5 = 10. What is m?
questions.explain: S = 6 + 9 + 3 + 7 + 10 = 35, and m = S / n = 35 / 5 = 7. The estimate m is the average of the sampled results.

questions.q: In the Monte Carlo sampling pseudocode that ends with m := S / n, what does n stand for?
choices: The size of the input array
The number of times the simulation is run
The largest sampled value
The probability of a correct answer
questions.explain: n is the number of simulation runs. S adds up the n results X_i, and m = S/n is their average.

questions.q: An algorithm estimates a quantity by running 10,000 random simulations and reporting the average result. Two separate executions may report slightly different numbers. What kind of algorithm is this?
choices: Las Vegas
Monte Carlo
Deterministic
Divide and conquer
questions.explain: It samples and averages, and its answer can differ between runs. That makes it Monte Carlo.

questions.q: Fill in the blank with one word: in a Monte Carlo algorithm, randomness can affect the answer; in a Las Vegas algorithm, randomness can affect the ____.
questions.explain: Las Vegas algorithms always give the correct answer, but how long they take can vary.

questions.q: In the Hiring Problem, you hire any candidate who is better than everyone interviewed so far. The applicants arrive in order from worst to best. How many people do you hire out of n applicants?
choices: about n/e
about n/2
n
questions.explain: Each new applicant beats everyone before them, so you hire all n of them and pay the hiring cost n times. It is the same kind of failure as Quick Sort on sorted input: a bad input order hurts you.

questions.q: Which statement describes the n/e strategy for the Hiring Problem?
choices: Hire the first applicant, then replace them whenever someone better appears
Interview the first n/e applicants without hiring any of them, then hire the first later applicant who is better than the best of that group
Interview n/e applicants chosen at random and hire the best of them
Hire the best of the first n/e applicants and stop interviewing
questions.explain: The first n/e applicants only set a benchmark (their maximum). After that, you hire the first applicant who beats that maximum.

questions.q: Under the n/e rule with n = 200 applicants, about how many applicants do you interview with no intention of hiring? Round to the nearest whole number.
questions.explain: e ≈ 2.718, so 200/e ≈ 73.6, which rounds to about 74. That is roughly the first 37% of applicants.

questions.q: True or false: the n/e rule always hires the best applicant.
questions.explain: It is a strategy, not a guarantee. For example, if a strong applicant who beats the benchmark shows up before the very best one, you hire that strong applicant and never reach the best.

questions.q: Hiring Problem with n = 10. Quality scores (higher is better) arrive in this order: [6, 2, 9, 4, 5, 8, 10, 3, 7, 1]. Using the n/e rule, you skip the first 4 applicants (10/e ≈ 3.68, rounded up). What is the score of the applicant you hire?
questions.explain: The first 4 are [6, 2, 9, 4], with maximum 9. Next come 5 (not better), 8 (not better), then 10 (better than 9), so you hire 10. This time the rule found the best applicant.

questions.q: One Hiring Problem strategy is to shuffle the applicants into a random order as they arrive. Why does this help?
choices: It guarantees that the best applicant comes first
It removes the cost of interviewing
It makes the worst-first ordering unlikely, the same idea as choosing a random pivot in Quick Sort
It lowers the number of applicants to n/e
questions.explain: Randomizing the input is a basic action you can apply to data. Like the random pivot, it takes away an adversary's ability to hand you the worst ordering.

questions.q: True or false: under the n/e rule, you hire the best applicant from the first group of n/e applicants.
questions.explain: Nobody in the first n/e group is hired. Their maximum only serves as the benchmark that a later applicant has to beat.

questions.q: Which formula gives the expected value of a discrete random variable X?
choices: E[X] = Σ_i P(X = x_i) · x_i
E[X] = Σ_i x_i
E[X] = Σ_i P(X = x_i)
E[X] = max_i x_i
questions.explain: Multiply each outcome's probability by its value, then add up the products.

questions.q: What is the expected value of one roll of a fair eight-sided die with faces 1 through 8?
True or false: the expected value of a random variable must be one of its possible outcomes.
questions.explain: A fair six-sided die has E[X] = 3.5, but you can never roll a 3.5.

questions.q: A factory makes a good phone worth $1000 with probability 499/500 and a bad phone worth -$5000 with probability 1/500. What is the expected value per phone, in dollars?
A game pays you $12 with probability 1/3 and costs you $3 (value -3) with probability 2/3. What is the expected value of one play, in dollars?
questions.explain: E[X] = (1/3)(12) + (2/3)(-3) = 4 - 2 = 2. Losses count as negative values.

questions.q: Which of these are discrete random variables?
choices: The number showing on a six-sided die
Tomorrow's rainfall in millimeters
The number of heads in 10 coin flips
A person's exact height
The temperature at noon
questions.explain: Die rolls and counts of heads come from a separate, countable set of values. Rainfall, height, and temperature can take any value in a range, so they are continuous.

questions.q: In the statement E[T(n)] = Θ(n log n) for Randomized Quick Sort, why is the running time T(n) treated as a random variable?
choices: Because the input array is always generated at random
Because T(n) depends on which pivots are randomly chosen
Because n itself is chosen at random
Because the sorted output is different on every run
questions.explain: On a fixed input, the amount of work depends on the random pivot choices, so T(n) is a random variable. Its expected value is Θ(n log n). The output is always the same correctly sorted array.
